beads.title: Clamp the EDNS size of a forwarded DNS query, as Go's forwarder does before it asks any resolver
beads.description: Go clamps the EDNS(0) requestor UDP payload size of a forwarded query before it goes on the wire, and this repository does not. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, net/dns/resolver/forwarder.go declares clampEDNSSize at line 198 and forwardWithDestChan calls it on the client's own query bytes at line 1238, rewriting the requestor size IN PLACE down to maxResponseBytes (4095; net/dns/resolver/tsdns.go line 50) before any resolver is asked. sendUDP calls it again on the answer at line 875. The clamp is deliberately partial: findOPTRecord (line 152) recognises only an OPT record at the very end of the message, with RDLEN == 0 and EDNS version 0, and clampEDNSSize returns without touching anything when it finds none. Go also deliberately does NOT clamp the TCP answer: the call is present but commented out at line 1056. This repository forwards the query byte for byte. ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs forward_query (line 1164) hands the client's query straight to ask_upstream_udp, and the module documentation at line 130 states the verbatim relay as a design fact rather than as a departure from Go; nothing rewrites the OPT record of the relayed answer either. Two consequences. RESOLVER-OBSERVABLE: a stub advertising 8192 makes this node put 8192 on the wire where a Go node puts 4095, so the resolver sizes its reply for a datagram this node cannot receive. The overlay netstack UDP receive ring is 4096 (netcore::Config::udp_buffer_size, not overridden here) and smoltcp drops an over-ring datagram at enqueue rather than delivering a short one. AND IT INTERACTS WITH THE RACE #462 JUST LANDED: that dropped datagram is now a failed UDP hop, so the name still resolves, but over a TCP connection to the resolver that a Go node would never have opened, and only after the two-second UDP_RACE_TIMEOUT. Before #462 it did not resolve at all. The pieces are already in the tree: find_opt_record (magic_dns.rs line 1038) is findOPTRecord with the same three restrictions, MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE (line 142) is maxResponseBytes, and cap_response (line 941) is already where the relayed answer is rewritten. The decision to make: clamp both sides as Go does, or only the outbound query. Note that 'clamp everything' is not the upstream behaviour, so a port that also clamps the TCP answer diverges in the other direction. Test the refusals, not only the clamp: a query whose OPT record is not last, or carries options (RDLEN != 0), or is an EDNS version this node will not act on, must be forwarded UNMODIFIED, exactly as find_opt_record already declines to read it; and a query already asking for 4095 or less must go out untouched. Assert on the bytes the forwarder actually sends, not on a re-derivation of them in the test body. Resolver-observable, not peer-observable. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Give a resolver that answers SERVFAIL or REFUSED the TCP hop Go gives it, instead of walking on
beads.description: A SERVFAIL or REFUSED answer from an upstream resolver wins the UDP/TCP race in this repository, where in Go it is an error that starts the TCP hop against the same resolver at once. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, net/dns/resolver/forwarder.go sendUDP does not return a soft-error answer: it returns rcodeResponseError{dns.RCodeServerFailure, out} at line 850 and rcodeResponseError{dns.RCodeRefused, out} at line 855 (the type is at line 767), an ERROR that carries the response bytes. firstUDP propagates it unchanged, and util/race/race.go Race.Start closes startFallback on any error from the first function (race.go line 102), so thenTCP dials the same resolver IMMEDIATELY rather than after udpRaceTimeout. The resolver therefore gets a second chance on a different transport before the query moves anywhere else, and the bytes reach forwardWithDestChan's error tally (line 1309 onward) only if TCP fails too. sendTCP does the same thing on its side (lines 1047 and 1052), so a resolver that refuses on both transports still ends as a refusal; the difference is only whether the second transport is tried at all. In this repository, ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs classify_udp (line 1300) reads exactly two things - does the datagram match the query, and did it fit - so a matching, well-fitting SERVFAIL or REFUSED becomes UdpOutcome::Answer, wins the race, and is returned by ask_upstream. forward_walk (line 1612) then applies is_soft_error (line 1145) and moves on to the NEXT upstream, having never asked this one over TCP. The port has a natural shape, because the truncation arm already is it: score a soft-error datagram the way UdpOutcome::Truncated is scored - hold the bytes, start the TCP hop, fall back to the held bytes if TCP brings nothing - which leaves forward_walk's existing soft-error precedence (first soft error held, relayed verbatim only once the list is exhausted, so an RFC 8914 extended DNS error survives) untouched. Two bounds are not optional. TcpRetry::Disabled (dns-forwarder-disable-tcp-retries) must shut this arm out exactly as it shuts out the truncation and slow-UDP arms - under it no TCP connection may be opened on any arm. And the anti-leak coupling stands: the TCP hop rides the overlay netstack Channel via channel.tcp_connect, never a host socket. Test the negative case as well: a resolver that answers REFUSED over UDP and REFUSED over TCP must still end as that refusal, with the upstream's own bytes relayed, and the walk must still move to the next upstream afterwards. The decision to make: port it, or record it as a deliberate divergence with its reason - a plausible reason exists, since the TCP retry of a refusal costs a connection for an answer that is unlikely to differ, but it is not written down anywhere today. Resolver-observable (a connection Go opens and this tree does not) and client-observable (a name that resolves over the refusing resolver's TCP path). See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Decide the upstream DNS walk: Go queries every resolver at once, this node queries them in turn
beads.description: This repository asks its upstream DNS resolvers one at a time; Go asks all of them at once. At commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, net/dns/resolver/forwarder.go forwardWithDestChan starts one goroutine per resolver at line 1282 and calls f.send from each at line 1293. The per-resolver startDelay (the resolverAndDelay field at line 287) is non-zero only for the well-known-DoH upgrades set at lines 423 to 439, which this fork has no upstream for, so in practice every resolver is queried simultaneously. The first success is taken off resc at line 1314; the error tally beginning at line 1309 acts only once numErr reaches len(resolvers) at line 1335. In this repository ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs forward_walk (line 1612) is a for loop that awaits one upstream's whole answer before the next is asked. Since #462 a dead resolver costs MORE than it used to: for a UDP client the UDP hop gets UDP_RACE_TIMEOUT alone (two seconds, line 1212), then the TCP hop starts and runs its own UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT (five seconds, line 96), so roughly seven seconds pass before the second resolver is tried, where Go answers at the healthy resolver's latency. Nothing bounds the walk as a whole - serve spawns the forward and UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT is per hop - so with two or more dead resolvers ahead of a healthy one the client's stub gives up long before this node reaches it, and the answer that eventually arrives is sent to a socket nobody is waiting on. THIS MAY WELL BE RIGHT TO KEEP, and that is the point of the entry. ask_upstream's own documentation calls walking on to the next upstream 'a second party learning a name it was never asked about', and Go's fan-out hands EVERY configured resolver EVERY query - a real privacy difference, and the kind of trade this fork makes deliberately elsewhere. What is missing is not the fan-out, it is the record: the divergence appears nowhere in PORTING.md, nowhere in forward_walk's doc comment as a divergence, and the ledger row that closed on forward_walk describes Go's behaviour as a walk, which it is not. The decision to make, explicitly: port the fan-out with Go's tally rules (first success wins; the soft-error preference applies only once every resolver has failed), or keep the sequential walk and write the privacy argument down in PORTING.md and at forward_walk with the latency cost stated. If the fan-out is ported, keep what forward_walk already gets right - the anti-poisoning source and question check before a response is eligible to be relayed OR remembered, the first soft error relayed verbatim ahead of the synthesized fallback, and every other RCODE (NXDOMAIN included) ending the forward where it is found - and bound the concurrency against MAX_INFLIGHT_FORWARDS, since N resolvers per query multiplies the overlay sockets a single client can pin. Client-observable (latency, and whether a name resolves at all before the stub gives up) and resolver-observable (which resolvers see the query). See PORTING.md section B.
